title: Glucose-HR coupling increases with diabetes severity
statement: Type 2 diabetes is associated with increased positive glucose-HR coupling, measurable from synchronized CGM and wearable HR streams, that increases monotonically with diabetes severity.
mechanism: In healthy physiology, glucose and heart rate are loosely coordinated through autonomic regulation and metabolic demand. As diabetes progresses, autonomic neuropathy and chronic hyperglycemia create a pathological positive feedback: elevated glucose drives sympathetic activation (raising HR), while impaired autonomic buffering fails to decouple the two signals. This produces tighter, more positive glucose-HR correlation that scales with disease severity.
predictions: Awake glucose-HR Pearson correlation increases monotonically across healthy -> pre-diabetes -> oral medication -> insulin-dependent groups
The coupling gradient survives adjustment for HbA1c, BMI, mean glucose, mean HR, total activity, and sleep fraction
Spearman and partial correlations show the same monotonic trend
Effect size (Cohen's d) for the linear severity contrast exceeds 0.5

literature.title: Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function
literature.key_finding: Introduced network physiology framework showing that inter-organ coupling structure changes with physiological state and sleep stages.
literature.relevance: Foundational framework for measuring glucose-HR coupling as a network physiology edge.

literature.title: Heart rate variability as a predictor of type 2 diabetes mellitus
literature.key_finding: Reduced HRV is an independent predictor of incident T2DM, indicating autonomic dysfunction precedes or accompanies metabolic disease.
literature.relevance: Supports the mechanistic link between autonomic dysregulation and diabetes that manifests as altered glucose-HR coupling.

feasibility.statistical_power: N=1939 with 4-group gradient provides >99% power for d=0.5
key_challenges: CGM and HR stream alignment across different device clocks
Confounding by raw glucose and HR levels
dataset_limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference about coupling changes over disease progression
10-day overlap window limits long-term coupling stability assessment

test_plan.primary_method: Kruskal-Wallis test across 4 diabetes severity groups with Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test, followed by pairwise comparisons with FDR correction
implementation_steps: Align CGM and HR streams to common 5-min grid per participant
Compute per-person Pearson, Spearman, and partial correlations (adjusting for activity and sleep) between glucose and HR during awake periods
Run Kruskal-Wallis test across healthy/pre-diabetes/oral/insulin groups
Compute Cohen's d for ordered severity contrast
Run sensitivity analyses adjusting for age, site, HbA1c, BMI, glucose mean, HR mean, activity total, sleep fraction
test_plan.success_criterion: FDR-significant monotonic increase in glucose-HR coupling across severity groups that survives confounder adjustment
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No significant difference across groups, or coupling decreases with severity, or effect disappears after HbA1c adjustment
sensitivity_checks: Adjustment for age and site only
Adjustment for raw glucose and HR means
Adjustment for activity and sleep fraction
secondary_methods: Partial correlation adjusting for physical activity and sleep
Stratification by awake vs sleep periods

results.method_used: Kruskal-Wallis with FDR correction, Cohen's d for ordered contrast, sensitivity analysis with progressive confounder adjustment

sensitivity_checks.name: Full confounder adjustment (age, site, HbA1c, BMI, glucose mean, HR mean, activity, sleep)

results.interpretation: Glucose-HR coupling increases monotonically with diabetes severity, transitioning from slightly negative (healthy) to positive (insulin-dependent). This reflects a pathological locking of metabolic and cardiac dynamics that intensifies with disease progression. The effect is robust to extensive confounder adjustment.
results.surprises: Direction was INCREASED coupling (more positive correlation), not decreased as expected from the classical 'decoupling' hypothesis in network physiology. Diabetes appears to create pathological hyper-coupling rather than disconnection.

issues: 10-day window may not capture full coupling dynamics
suggestions: Validate in longitudinal cohort if available
Stratify by medication class to assess pharmacological confounding
Test circadian variation of the coupling signal

notes: Flagship finding of the coupling atlas analysis. The direction of the effect (increased coupling, not decreased) is the key surprise and differentiates this from the standard decoupling narrative.
